# Omni View North America
> **Nine hundred forty-three measles cases and a fifth death are straining Pennsylvania's counties.**

**What You Need to Know:** Pennsylvania health officials are preparing for measles to move past the counties already hit, after the state reported a fifth measles-associated death and 943 confirmed cases. In Quebec, Coalition Avenir Québec leader Christine Fréchette is asking voters for a first mandate as premier while centering the trade fight with the United States. In Hawaii, more than a third of this year's 98 general-election races have a candidate with no opponent.

### Lead
**Pennsylvania health officials brace themselves as measles outbreak expected to spread: The Guardian**
Last week Pennsylvania reported its fifth measles-associated death amid 943 confirmed cases across 39 counties, The Guardian reports. Some public health officials say it is only a matter of time before the disease moves beyond the outbreak's epicenter. Only seven of the state's 67 counties have their own health department. Lancaster County, which has none, has the most cases, 381, believed to be mostly among Amish or similar religious groups with historically low uptake of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, and local doctors and community members are trying to create a county health department. Jeanne Franklin, director of the Chester County health department, said her county has the third-highest total, 83 cases, shares a long border with Lancaster, and is preparing for the virus to reach people outside Plain communities even as the county tries to stop that. She said many Amish residents were unvaccinated because they were unaware of the shot or seek care less often, not because they reject vaccines, and that they will decide from what is happening to neighbors. Chester County is running surveillance, contact tracing and community vaccination sites, and working to counter misinformation about vaccine safety. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/04/pennsylvania-health-officials-measles-outbreak)

### Across the Region
**Christine Fréchette faces first provincial election test as CAQ leader: Yahoo Finance Canada**
Christine Fréchette is seeking her first electoral mandate as Quebec premier, less than six months after succeeding François Legault at the head of the Coalition Avenir Québec, in power since 2018. Across a 39-day campaign she has argued for a change in leadership without a change in government, and at the launch she named US President Donald Trump her real opponent in the trade war, saying she was asking for a mandate to move forward through the storm. She has campaigned on affordability, health care and support for families and seniors, including more money for home care and school-related expenses. She has appealed to sovereigntists who do not want a referendum amid economic uncertainty and to Liberal voters worried about a Parti Québécois government, calling herself an autonomist and declining to say how she would vote on sovereignty. After the third leaders' debate she called for an urgent meeting with Prime Minister Mark Carney and warned that Americans might secretly be trying to support the Parti Québécois to destabilize Canada; hours later she said there was no evidence of foreign interference. Source: [ca.finance.yahoo.com](https://ca.finance.yahoo.com/news/christine-fr-chette-faces-first-100023538.html)

**Beth Fukumoto: When Politicians Run Unopposed, Everyone Loses: Honolulu Civil Beat**
Of Hawaii's 98 general-election races this year, from Congress to county council, more than a third will feature a candidate with no opposition, Honolulu Civil Beat reports. Senate President Ron Kouchi and House Speaker Nadine Nakamura have already secured their seats with no opponent, and in 24 races only one candidate ran from start to finish. In 27 percent of this year's legislative races only one candidate ever ran, so voters never had a choice, and nearly half of those legislative races were settled without a general-election contest. When only one candidate advances from the primary, Hawaii declares that person the winner and the race never appears on the November ballot, and the state is one of six that do not allow write-in votes, according to a 2023 report from the US Election Assistance Commission. Ballotpedia found that 28,032 of 40,800 elections it tracked through August, about 69 percent, were uncontested. Source: [civilbeat.org](https://www.civilbeat.org/2026/10/how-hawaii-can-combat-uncontested-elections/)

### Also Today
**Kristi Noem’s Agency Gave Her Donor a Lucrative Contract Just Before She Left: The New York Times**
On Kristi Noem's last day as homeland security secretary, the department signed a multi-million-dollar agreement to buy five aircraft from a company owned by a political contributor to her, documents show, The New York Times reports. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/04/us/politics/kristi-noem-planes-donor.html)

**Conservative US supreme court justice Samuel Alito hints at retirement in interview: The Guardian**
Justice Samuel Alito, 76, told CBS in an interview scheduled to air Monday that he thinks he has to contemplate retiring every year, after considering it at the end of the term that ended in June and deciding he could still contribute. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/04/samuel-alito-supreme-court-interview)

**Cornell University to take ‘serious look’ at fraternities after rape allegations: The Guardian**
Cornell's president said Saturday the university will examine fraternities and sororities after a woman alleged she was drugged and raped in 2024 by several members of the Chi Phi fraternity in Ithaca, New York. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/04/cornell-president-vows-serious-look-at-fraternities-in-wake-of-allegations)

**She died covering war for Fox News. Her parents blame the network — and a star reporter: NPR**
Family members of two Fox News journalists killed while covering the war in Ukraine are suing the network, saying it put getting the story ahead of its people. Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/10/04/nx-s1-5737621/fox-news-ukraine-deaths)

### The Region and the World
**Trump's nominee for Hostage Affairs envoy faces scrutiny on controversial Russia plan: The Hill**
President Trump is tapping John Coale, his former lawyer and special envoy to Belarus, as the US official charged with bringing home unjustly detained Americans, The Hill reports. Coale has helped free hundreds of political prisoners from Belarus. He has described vodka-infused negotiations with that country's leader, Alexander Lukashenko. The Hill says the nominee faces scrutiny over a controversial Russia plan. Source: [thehill.com](https://thehill.com/policy/international/6124543-trump-hostage-affairs-coale-belarus-russia-ukraine/)

### Both Sides: Whether state courts can hear climate suits against oil companies
The US Supreme Court hears oral arguments Monday in Suncor Energy versus Boulder County, on whether federal law stops the city and county of Boulder, Colorado, from suing Suncor Energy and Exxon Mobil in state court. Boulder sued under state law to hold the companies responsible for costs tied to climate disasters, arguing they deceived the public about the danger of their products. The Colorado Supreme Court ruled that federal law does not stand in the way of the claims moving forward in state court. Jonathan Adler, a professor at William and Mary Law School who filed a brief, said that if this path closes too, seeking court remedies will be largely off the table, because a 2011 Supreme Court decision already left little future for similar cases in federal court. Suncor and Exxon told the justices they have a chance to decide whether the litigation can proceed before the energy industry is threatened with potentially enormous judgments. Similar claims have been filed in Vermont, Minnesota and Hawaii, and courts have split on whether federal law preempts them. The companies' filing and Boulder's suit both treat the procedural answer as one that could shape claims from dozens of states, counties and cities seeking billions of dollars for fires, floods and other climate-disaster costs. Monday's argument is the next step the reporting names. Source: [notus.org](https://www.notus.org/climate-environment/supreme-court-fossil-fuel-lawsuit-change)

**Oregon Man Pinned by Boulder Calls 911 Using Siri From His Earbuds: The New York Times**
In Oregon, a man pinned under a boulder that police said likely weighed a literal ton called 911 through Apple's Siri on his earbuds because he could not reach his phone, his mother told The New York Times. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/04/us/oregon-man-pinned-boulder-siri-rescue.html)

# Omni View North America
> **A judge froze wall construction across five hundred miles of the Texas-Mexico border.**

**What You Need to Know:** A judge froze wall construction across five hundred miles of the Texas-Mexico border. Judge Kathleen Cardone’s preliminary injunction bars federal agencies from building barriers or disturbing ground in the Big Bend Sector until they comply with applicable laws. The order covers about a quarter of the U.S.-Mexico border, including Big Bend National Park.

### Lead
**Trump Suffers Legal Setback As Texas Border Wall Blocked In National Park: Newsweek**
On Friday, Judge Kathleen Cardone of the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Texas ordered a temporary halt to border-wall construction and related infrastructure in the Big Bend region. The preliminary injunction says federal agencies shall not build a border barrier or related infrastructure, or do any construction or ground-disturbing work, in the Big Bend Sector until they comply with all applicable laws. The order covers the entire sector, about 500 miles and roughly a quarter of the U.S.-Mexico border, including Big Bend National Park, which the National Park Service says has 118 miles of border with Mexico. Cardone concluded that a coalition of environmental groups and local landowners is likely to succeed on at least one claim. The court did not decide the underlying case for construction in the sector. Source: [newsweek.com](https://www.newsweek.com/trump-suffers-legal-setback-as-texas-border-wall-blocked-in-national-park-12519989)

### Across the Region
**B.C. candidates and voters scramble to get their minds around two elections, one week apart: The Globe and Mail**
British Columbia is holding municipal and provincial elections in the same month for the first time since the province’s Election Act was passed in 1995. In Surrey, more than 380,000 eligible voters are asked to choose a mayor, eight councillors and six school trustees on October 17, then an MLA on October 24, sifting through nearly 100 municipal candidates and at least 20 provincial candidates across 10 ridings. Premier David Eby called the provincial vote as a snap election on September 22, after municipal races had already been planned for years. The Globe and Mail reports that experts warn turnout could suffer, especially municipally, and that two upstart right-wing parties say they will compete in a majority of the 93 ridings after the provincial Conservatives splintered and partly reunified. Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-bc-candidates-and-voters-scramble-to-get-their-minds-around-two/)

**‘It’s enraging’: lawmakers call for action after Guardian investigation into convenience store overcharges: The Guardian**
Five members of the U.S. House have called out pricing at 7-Eleven and Circle K after The Guardian found the chains frequently charge more at the register or pump than shelf tags or outdoor fuel signs promise. Representative Becca Balint, a Democrat from Vermont, said customers are being forced to fact-check every price, and she asked the Federal Trade Commission to investigate and to hold the companies accountable if they are deliberately misleading customers. Representative Nanette Barragán, a Democrat whose district covers part of Los Angeles County, called the findings disturbing and said President Trump and Republicans are raising the cost of food and necessities. Between 2023 and 2025, The Guardian’s review of inspections found 7-Eleven failed 41 percent of price inspections in Arizona and 47 percent in both Colorado and Utah, while Circle K failed 35 percent in Florida, 39 percent in Arizona and 62 percent in North Carolina. The chains did not answer The Guardian’s questions; President Trump has called affordability concerns a “hoax” and a “con job,” and an AP-NORC poll released Thursday found 17 percent of Americans approve of his handling of the cost of living. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/03/convenience-store-overcharges-us-congress)

### Also Today
**Senate Races in Republican States Tilt Toward Democrats, Polls Find: The New York Times**
New York Times/Siena polls found Democrats performing strongly in five reliably Republican states where they are trying to flip Senate seats. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/03/us/senate-polls-texas-kansas-ohio-alaska-iowa.html)

**The Supreme Court faces another term jam-packed with controversy: NPR**
The Supreme Court term opens Monday with test cases on religion, guns and climate change, and with the emergency docket still active. Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/10/03/nx-s1-5986341/supreme-court-term-religion-guns-environment-immigration)

**The American dream remains elusive in the valley that inspired East of Eden: The Guardian**
A Brookings Institution analysis found Salinas, California, the least affordable city in the United States for the middle class. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/03/salinas-california-john-steinbeck)

**A record number of Native Americans are running in the 2026 midterms: The Washington Post**
The Washington Post reports that a record number of Native Americans are running in the 2026 midterms. Source: [washingtonpost.com](https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/10/03/record-number-native-americans-are-running-2026-midterms/)

### The Region and the World
**‘It’s been hard’: families await the return of the USS Abraham Lincoln: The Guardian**
The USS Abraham Lincoln is expected to dock in San Diego this week after what The Guardian calls a record-breaking deployment of more than 250 days at sea. Sailors’ relatives say they are relieved. A mother in San Diego said she had a big welcome sign made and that she cannot wait to see her son. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-interactive/2026/oct/03/uss-abraham-lincoln-returns-from-deployment)

### Both Sides: Should wall work resume in Big Bend before the laws are met?
Whether federal agencies may build a border wall and related works in Texas’s Big Bend sector before they comply with environmental and other laws is the question left by Friday’s preliminary injunction from Judge Kathleen Cardone.

The plaintiffs, a coalition of environmental groups and local landowners, want the work kept stopped. The reason Cardone said carries them — that they are likely to succeed on at least one claim — is that they face serious, irreparable harm without an injunction, and that the balance of the equities and the public interest weigh in their favor until the government meets all applicable laws.

President Trump’s stated priority, as Newsweek describes it, is reducing illegal crossings of the southern border, which he has made one of the main aims of his presidency. His 2025 law, which the article calls the Big Beautiful Bill, earmarked $46.5 billion for fencing and other obstacles along the 1,954-mile southern border. Planned works include hundreds of miles of 30-foot wall, surveillance systems and river barriers, on private land as well as federal land. In August, bulldozers were seen clearing land in Big Bend National Park, which the article says sparked anger across parties.

# Omni View North America
> **Two failed injections stopped Tennessee's remaining executions for the rest of the year.**

**What You Need to Know:** Two failed lethal injections have stopped Tennessee's remaining executions for the rest of the year. Governor Bill Lee ordered the pause after Christa Gail Pike survived Wednesday's attempt and was taken to hospital. It is the state's second botched execution this year.

### Lead
**Tennessee governor halts executions after second botched lethal injection attempt this year: The Guardian US**
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has halted the state's remaining executions for the rest of the year after officials were unable to put Christa Gail Pike to death on Wednesday. Pike, sentenced to death over a 1995 murder of a schoolmate, was taken to hospital after surviving two lethal injections. Witnesses said she was still breathing and was heard snoring about 40 minutes after the doses meant to kill her. The Guardian reports it is the second botched execution in Tennessee this year. The pause covers the executions still scheduled for the rest of 2026. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live/2026/oct/01/tennessee-governor-halts-executions-christa-pike-lethal-injection-donald-trump-hegseth-musk-us-politics-latest-news-updates)

### Across the Region
**Carney heads to Fort McMurray to announce ‘next steps’ for proposed West Coast pipeline: iPolitics**
Eleven months after the Canada–Alberta memorandum, Prime Minister Mark Carney is in Fort McMurray today with Premier Danielle Smith. Canadian Press, cited by iPolitics, reports he is expected to confirm that the proposed West Coast pipeline will be designated a project of national interest under the Building Canada Act — the first such designation since Bill C-5 passed more than a year ago. His itinerary says only that he will announce the next step to accelerate a major infrastructure project, at 9 a.m. Mountain Time. Ottawa posted its intent in the Canada Gazette in August and said Indigenous consultation was already underway. Energy Minister Tim Hodgson told the Globe and Mail he expects the Major Projects Office to finish on time so the designation can be issued. Source: [ipolitics.ca](https://www.ipolitics.ca/2026/10/01/carney-heads-to-fort-macmurray-to-announce-next-steps-for-proposed-west-coast-pipeline/)

**Trump officials abandon effort to investigate election threats, experts warn: The Guardian US**
Former officials and a recent report say the Trump administration has abandoned key bodies meant to investigate direct threats to U.S. elections by foreign actors and domestic terrorists, while officials have focused on unsubstantiated claims of widespread voter fraud by noncitizens. Nikki Fisher, former chief election security officer for the Oregon secretary of state, said the Justice Department's election-threats task force prosecuted 21 cases from 2021 to 2024, including Solomon Peña and Quintez Brown, and now appears defunct in practice, with no new cases prosecuted. Her June paper, written at the Naval Postgraduate School, said the task force received more than 2,000 reports and opened more than 100 investigations in those years. Asked about the task force, the department pointed to nine releases in the past five weeks on indictments of foreign nationals for election fraud and stolen identities. The day after Pam Bondi's confirmation as attorney general, she eliminated the FBI's foreign-influence task force. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/01/trump-us-election-threats)

### Also Today
**New Facility at Louisiana Airport to Hold Immigrant Children and Families: The New York Times US**
The New York Times reports a new site at an airport in Alexandria, Louisiana, will hold immigrant children and families, expanding what it calls the Trump administration's busiest deportation hub in order to streamline and accelerate removals. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/01/us/ice-child-detention-center-louisiana.html)

**A high-stakes fight for state political power heats up, with Trump's agenda on the line: KTVN**
Voters in 46 states will choose more than 6,100 lawmakers in November, about 83 percent of legislative seats nationwide, and 36 states will hold gubernatorial elections, the National Conference of State Legislatures says. Source: [ktvn.com](http://www.ktvn.com/news/national/a-high-stakes-fight-for-state-political-power-heats-up-with-trumps-agenda-on-the/article_d3792d84-ab2b-5680-af20-31a79c68ca2c.html)

**Fed's Warsh seeks to avoid forward guidance. His colleagues aren't listening: The Hill**
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh has tried, over four-plus months in the job, to stop the central bank from forecasting its own decisions, The Hill reports, but after a rate increase earlier this month several officials have indicated further hikes are coming. Source: [thehill.com](https://thehill.com/business/6121513-warsh-forward-guidance-fed-rate-hikes/)

### The Region and the World
**Calls for gas tax suspensions grow as Americans struggle with high prices: The Hill**
Gasoline near $4.50 a gallon, which The Hill ties to the Iran war, is driving new calls in the United States to suspend federal and state fuel taxes. The Hill reports those calls are gaining momentum as Americans struggle with pump prices elevated by the seven-month conflict. Indiana and Georgia this week have either suspended or reduced their own fuel taxes. The fight is over who absorbs the war's cost at the pump: drivers now, or state and federal fuel-tax revenue. Source: [thehill.com](https://thehill.com/business/6121887-calls-for-gas-tax-suspensions-grow-as-americans-struggle-with-high-prices/)

### Both Sides: Who pays when a police chase that broke the rules ends in a death
The question is whether Chicago must pay all of a $10.5 million jury award when officers broke pursuit rules and the driver they chased was also found at fault. The Illinois Supreme Court on Wednesday refused to hear the city's appeal. That refusal becomes final in 21 days and leaves standing a First District Appellate Court ruling that the city pays the entire verdict. Tuong Lam, 61, died on April 13, 2018, near Devon and Kedzie avenues in Lincolnwood, struck by the driver police were chasing. A Cook County jury set the $10.5 million figure in 2023 for his wife and three children.

Lawyers for the city argue the chased driver should pay a share. Their strongest reason is that he was found partially responsible for the crash, so taxpayers should not cover fault a jury assigned to him.

Lawyers for Lam's family argue the city should pay the whole sum. Their strongest reason is that officers violated the Chicago Police Department's 2018 pursuit policy: they chased a driver wanted only on suspicion of a traffic violation, in an unmarked vehicle, without telling dispatchers, and without weighing whether an immediate arrest outweighed the danger of the chase. The appellate court agreed the city owes the full amount.

Both sides accept the jury's $10.5 million figure and the finding that the driver was partly at fault. In February a city lawyer told the City Council Finance Committee that the Supreme Court outcome would profoundly affect other pursuit lawsuits. A spokesperson for the Chicago Department of Law declined to comment. WTTW reports the rejection is likely to leave Chicago paying the full cost of similar suits when a pursuit broke policy, whether or not the person chased was at fault. Source: [news.wttw.com](https://news.wttw.com/2026/10/01/chicago-must-pay-105m-family-man-killed-driver-being-chased-police-supreme-court-ruling)

> **Three months early, Montana ties Medicaid coverage to proof of work, volunteering, or study.**

**What You Need to Know:** Three months early, Montana ties Medicaid coverage to proof of work, volunteering, or study. Enforcement begins October 1, while most states wait until January 1, and NPR reports the early start is sowing confusion and anxiety. Ontario has spent $140 million from a $5 billion tariff account, and the Senate is holding procedural votes on a data-center energy bill the House passed 417-3.

### Lead
**Montana starts enforcing Medicaid work requirements on Oct 1. Patients are confused: NPR**
Montana begins enforcing Medicaid work requirements on October 1. In most states, people with Medicaid coverage must prove they are working, volunteering, or studying starting January 1. Montana is starting that requirement three months sooner. NPR reports the early start is sowing confusion and anxiety among patients. Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/09/30/nx-s1-5946766/montana-early-medicaid-work-requirements-patients-confused)

### Across the Region
**Ford government ‘Protect Ontario’ tariff program spent $140 million so far: Global News**
Nearly two years into an escalating trade battle with the United States, Premier Doug Ford’s $5 billion Protect Ontario account has spent $140 million to shore up tariff-hit businesses, Global News reported. At a Tuesday committee at Queen’s Park, Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy tried to treat questions about that spending as outside his scope, then left the figures to Deputy Minister of Finance Gadi Mayman. Mayman said 36 applications totaling just under $100 million had been received, 18 had been approved for about $40 million, and Algoma Steel support added $100 million. Liberal finance critic Stephanie Bowman said only $40 million had gone to help businesses — 0.01 per cent of provincial GDP, in her telling — and that the program is not working. Bethlenfalvy pointed to other supports he said had seen uptake, and the government has said it would move billions from the account into an investment fund run by a private-sector partner. Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12077838/ford-government-protect-ontario-tariff-program-spent-140-million-so-far/)

**Donor Gives $3 Billion to Carnegie Mellon, the Largest University Gift Ever: The New York Times**
Hedge fund executive Kenneth C. Griffin pledged to give $3 billion to Carnegie Mellon University, The New York Times reported. The Times described the pledge as the largest university gift ever. Much of the money is to build a campus in Miami. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/us/3-billion-donation-carnegie-mellon-largest-university-gift.html)

### Also Today
**A startup wants to build a massive nuclear-powered data center on public land in Utah: NPR**
Valar Atomics wants to place over 450 reactors on more than 9,500 acres of public land in Utah to power a data center. Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/09/30/nx-s1-5983482/valar-atomic-nuclear-data-center-project-beehive-utah)

**New Orleans judge files criminal case against CBS affiliate over reporting: The Guardian**
Criminal Court Judge Kimya Holmes filed a police complaint against a CBS affiliate over a segment on a real-estate deal she was involved in, invoking a law that no longer carries criminal penalties, journalist David Hammer said. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/30/new-orleans-judge-criminal-case-cbs-affiliate)

**Trump campaign ads paid with public money violate federal law, critics say: The Guardian**
Public Citizen asked the FCC and the FTC to stop three White House ads promoting Donald Trump that the group says illegally use public funds; the White House calls them public service announcements. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/30/trump-campaign-ads-violate-federal-law)

**55 Swatting Calls: A Couple’s Fight Against Online Stalkers and the Police: The New York Times**
Milwaukee agreed to a $575,000 settlement after heavily armed police responses to 55 hoax 911 calls to a couple’s home that officials knew were hoaxes. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/us/swatting-milwaukee-couple-settlement.html)

### Both Sides: Should the Senate advance the data-center ratepayer bill before November?
The question on September 30 is whether the Senate should advance the House-passed Ratepayer Protection Act, on data-center energy costs, before November’s midterms. A second House bill, cracking down on congressional stock trading and carrying a voter-identification mandate, is on the same procedural slate.

Senator Jon Husted, an Ohio Republican and the ratepayer bill’s author, said the measure cleared the House 417-3 and is “the only bill that has a chance to get to the president’s desk before we get to the election.” He said it will be up to Democrats “whether or not they want to play politics or they want to solve affordability issues,” and he tied that choice to power costs in Ohio. Republican leaders hope the votes let vulnerable senators say they backed cost-of-living and corruption measures. Punchbowl News reported that even some Republican senators doubt that will matter this late.

Punchbowl News reported Senate Democrats are likely to block both bills. Senator John Hickenlooper, a Colorado Democrat, said that in the House “it’s so easy and people go along with these symbolic things there that have no teeth,” and that “the Senate doesn’t work that way.” The outlet reported Democrats do not appear worried about rejecting a bill nearly all House Democrats supported.

President Donald Trump, at a Tuesday White House news conference with technology executives including Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, said the companies would be “very generous with communities.” He declared that once data centers arrived, “taxes have gone down,” “incomes have gone up,” and “the value of their housing has gone up.” Punchbowl News reported that earlier this year he got technology giants to pledge to shield residents from higher energy costs — the idea behind the bill — and has since defended the facilities as voters have soured on them.

Both sides are dealing with a bill the House already passed 417-3. Three procedural votes were set for 11:30 a.m., one on each bill and one Cabinet nomination, after which senators could be free until mid-November. Source: [punchbowl.news](https://punchbowl.news/article/senate/senate-votes-midterm-elections/)

**Judge Ends Federal Oversight of Oakland Police After 23 Years: The New York Times**
A federal court ended federal oversight of the Oakland Police Department after 23 years, the longest such monitoring in U.S. history, saying the department had mostly complied with reforms required by a 2003 settlement that followed a police brutality lawsuit. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/us/oakland-police-reform-federal-oversight.html)

# Omni View North America
> **Six thousand U.S. job ads still require a political essay a judge has barred.**

**What You Need to Know:** Six thousand U.S. job ads still require a political essay a judge has barred. Judge George A. O'Toole Jr. stayed the prompt on September 11, the Justice Department says new announcements cannot include it, and agencies were told to ignore answers on older postings. Ontario's premier, separately, offered patient capital for a pipeline from Alberta to Sarnia.

### Lead
**Federal hiring ads still carry a political essay after a judge's stay: Dagens.com**
On September 11, Judge George A. O'Toole Jr. stayed a Trump administration hiring prompt that asked applicants to explain how they would advance the president's agenda and to name their favorite executive orders, finding it likely unconstitutional. In a Friday court filing, the Justice Department said human resources departments cannot include the political essay in new job announcements. Officials say deleting the text by hand from roughly six thousand active postings would disrupt the hiring system, so agencies were ordered to ignore submitted answers. Managers must use a revised prompt asking candidates to describe a time they followed leadership directions that differed from their own recommendations. The White House introduced the essay in May 2025 and later made it optional after backlash from civil servants; ethics groups had argued that civil-service hiring must rest on merit. Source: [dagens.com](https://www.dagens.com/news/insider-reveals-trump-admin-keeps-defying-judges-order-5-times-in-two-weeks)

### Across the Region
**Ford says Ontario willing to bankroll a pipeline from Alberta to Sarnia: Financial Post**
Ontario Premier Doug Ford told a Calgary luncheon on Monday that the province is willing to finance the proposed Northern Shield pipeline, which would move up to 500,000 barrels a day from Hardisty, Alberta, to Sarnia, Ontario. > **Six months after a softer-touch pledge, ICE still arrests people in daily American life.**

**What You Need to Know:** Six months after a softer-touch pledge, ICE is still arresting people during ordinary errands across the United States, The Guardian reports. A Venezuelan man was put on a flight and then taken off before takeoff after officers said they may have erred, and an agent shot an asylum seeker in Austin last week. Colorado voters will decide whether the state may keep more revenue for schools, and Walmart’s chief executive said digital shelf tags will not be used to charge different people different prices.

### Lead
**Gone in 90 seconds: an ‘invisibilized’ ICE is arresting more people than ever: The Guardian**
President Donald Trump said in February that he had learned the agency “could use a little bit of a softer touch,” after officers killed two U.S. citizens during an ICE operation in Minneapolis and public backlash followed, The Guardian reports. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, at his Senate confirmation hearing in March, said his goal in six months was that the department not lead the news every day, after earlier raids that residents described as a siege, with armored vehicles in neighborhoods and agents outside elementary schools. The Guardian describes a Cuban man detained in Miami just after he took out the trash, an Ecuadorian father arrested in Danbury, Connecticut, after he saw his six-year-old onto the school bus, and people taken while pumping gas, their cars left behind. A Venezuelan man identified as Y was stopped at Phoenix Sky Harbor; he said officers would not say why he was being arrested or accept a judicial order barring deportation to Venezuela, and four days later he was placed on a plane, then removed before takeoff after ICE officers said they may have made a mistake. Last week an ICE agent shot Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez in Austin, Texas; the Venezuelan asylum seeker, who had a deportation order after missing a letter to appear in immigration court, was discharged with a bullet still lodged near his spine and then taken to ICE detention. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-interactive/2026/sep/28/ice-us-immigration-new-tactics)

Democratic majorities sent it to voters in May, a break from 2024, when lawmakers referred seven questions, and from an average of about five in every even-year election since 2016. Nonpartisan state analysts estimate the higher cap would increase K-12 funding by about $500 million a year and, depending on later revenue growth, could shrink Taxpayer’s Bill of Rights refunds. The measure passed the Legislature mostly on party lines, with nearly all Democrats in favor and Republicans unanimously opposed; Colorado Education Association president Kevin Vick has said it does not raise taxes and would let the state use revenue it already collects for students and educators. Yes For Colorado Kids, the committee registered in support, had reported just under $2 million in contributions as of Sept. 1. Source: [coloradonewsline.com](https://coloradonewsline.com/2026/09/28/cap-revenue-colorado-ballot-measure/)

**Walmart vows no surge pricing as digital shelf tags sweep stores: The Independent**
Walmart chief executive John Furner wrote on the company website Friday that the retailer does not set different prices based on who a shopper is or the time of day, and will not, The Independent reports. He said Walmart does not use income, shopping history, or a customer’s willingness to spend to set prices, and will not do so, and that the same rule binds Sparky, its artificial-intelligence shopping assistant, which he said will not raise a price for one customer or hide a lower-priced option that fits the search. Furner said those practices would conflict with the company’s “everyday low prices” model, while prices can still fall when costs fall or rise when goods cost more to source or ship. In March, Walmart said 2,300 of its U.S. stores were using digital shelf labels, with a plan to expand them company-wide over the next year. Last month the Federal Trade Commission warned that personalizing prices could violate consumer-protection standards. ### Both Sides: Whether Idaho should host spent nuclear fuel
Idaho legislators are making the case for a federal Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus, and the decision in front of the state is whether to seek a U.S. Department of Energy site that would store spent fuel. The Idaho Capital Sun reports that if Idaho were selected, the state would have to accept and store spent nuclear fuel and radioactive waste.

Senator Dave Lent, a Republican from Idaho Falls and a retired Idaho National Laboratory training manager, says the state is unusually well placed because of the laboratory’s 75-year record of research, safety, and innovation. He says researchers and engineers there already take spent fuel, reprocess it, and turn it into new reactor fuel. On workforce, location, facilities, and expertise, he calls Idaho a standout possible host, and he says the hard part is helping residents understand what high-level waste is and how it can be handled safely. More than 40 Idaho legislators have voiced support. Governor Brad Little has said, in the campus talks, that protecting the Snake River aquifer is nonnegotiable.

Representative Monica Church, a Democrat from Boise, opposes the project. She says that if three states are chosen, each could be responsible for accepting about 33,000 tons of the country’s spent nuclear fuel and radioactive waste. The Sun’s series says opponents argue against bringing the project to Idaho. Laboratory officials declined to be interviewed. The shared ground is that hosting would mean accepting and storing spent fuel; the dispute is whether Idaho should take that on. The Sun’s report on the opponents is set to conclude Tuesday. ### Both Sides: Hawaii’s handgun permit window and inspection rule
Hawaii’s handgun buyers are living with two rules a federal appeals court has just kept in force: thirty days to use a permit to acquire a handgun, and a requirement that some newly acquired guns be brought to a police station for inspection. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit upheld both in a 6-5 opinion. The state Department of the Attorney General announced the result.

The strongest case for keeping the rules is the one the majority wrote. Hawaii, the ruling explains, is a shall-issue state: an applicant who satisfies objective requirements may obtain a permit. Guided by the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2022 decision in New York State Rifle and Pistol Association v. Bruen, the en banc court held that this system fits the Second Amendment because the plaintiffs failed to show that the two provisions, which the majority called presumptively lawful, have been put toward abusive ends that would effectively deny ordinary citizens their rights.

The strongest case against is the lawsuit Todd Yukutake and David Kikukawa filed in 2019. They challenged the narrow window as unconstitutional. They also challenged a form asking for information about the firearm, and the duty, in certain circumstances, to bring that firearm to a police station for inspection. Their reason is that those steps still limit acquiring a gun after the state has found that the applicant qualifies.

What both accounts share is the shall-issue frame the ruling sets out: meeting the state’s objective requirements is what opens the door to a permit. The opinion leaves the thirty-day clock and the inspection mandate standing. > **A Pentagon office would own a third of a Venezuelan oil firm Trump says will refill US reserves.**

**What You Need to Know:** A Pentagon office would own a third of a Venezuelan oil firm that President Donald Trump says will refill US reserves, a structure experts told The Guardian the law blocks and that will not restock the reserve soon. The paper ties the August announcement to the January seizure of Nicolás Maduro and to claims it says do not survive Venezuelan or US legal limits. Elsewhere, Ottawa is sealing a Havana diplomats’ lawsuit, and Florida’s District 46 is a three-way rematch.

### Lead
**The truth behind Donald Trump’s ‘biggest oil deal in world history’: The Guardian**
The Guardian reports that an August plan for the Pentagon’s office of strategic capital to hold a third of North American Blue Energy Partners — a deal President Donald Trump called “the biggest oil deal in world history” — is almost certainly doomed on legal and logistical grounds. US forces seized Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January, the paper reports, moved him to a federal holding facility in the United States, and left Delcy Rodríguez in his place. Experts and officials who spoke with The Guardian said virtually everything Trump and his cabinet have said about the deal is false or misleading: Venezuelan law does not allow oil deals longer than 25 years, and the office is not authorized in US law to own company shares. They said the structure will not bring new capital into Venezuela’s oil sector and, contrary to Trump, will not refill the Strategic Petroleum Reserve any time soon; The Guardian reports the reserve fell to a longtime low after the US invaded Iran.

### Across the Region
**Canadians were spying for U.S. in Cuba at time of alleged sonic attacks: The Globe and Mail**
The Globe and Mail reports that Ottawa denies Canadians were spying in Cuba, while two unnamed sources told the paper a Canadian diplomat in Havana gathered human intelligence and sometimes shared it with American spies, and that Canadians used satellite equipment the United States brought in, between 2016 and 2018, as diplomats began reporting nosebleeds, dizziness, headaches, blurred vision and memory loss. The Department of Justice confirmed Friday that the government invoked Section 38 of the Canada Evidence Act to keep new details of the diplomats’ multimillion-dollar lawsuit secret; the paper says the sources are unnamed because disclosure could bring charges under the Foreign Interference and Security of Information Act. A court order sealing information was issued in April 2025, after an amended claim in August 2024. Lead lawyer Paul Miller declined specifics under that order and said there was a fear that things said in court could be of national security sensitivity. Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/politics/article-canadians-spying-for-us-in-cuba-at-time-alleged-sonic-attacks-source/)

**Threeway contest for Osceola-Orange state House seat a rematch of 2024: Orlando Sentinel**

Alvarez won in 2024 with 57 percent, Cruz 39.6 percent and Rivera 3.4 percent; on August 18 he took 66 percent of the Democratic primary against Robert LeWayne Johnson. State records cited by the Orlando Sentinel put Democrats at 42 percent of registered voters and Republicans at about 21 percent. Alvarez, a former Kissimmee mayor and a Biden-era regional administrator at the US Department of Housing and Urban Development for the Southeast and Caribbean, says a second term would stay on affordable housing, healthcare and public safety, citing a veterans housing bill, vertiport funding and a recall process for community development boards. He opposes Amendment 3, which needs 60 percent of voters to create a $150,000 homestead exemption in 2027, rising to $250,000 in 2028, and to limit local spending to core services; he says legislative backers could not explain how governments would offset lost revenue, and he expects the November vote to shape the session that starts in March. ### Both Sides: Ontario's property assessment freeze

In 2020, at the height of COVID-19, the province ordered the Municipal Property Assessment Corporation to pause. The Globe and Mail reports the system was never switched back on.

Paul Sullivan, a British Columbia property-tax consultant and national tax leader at Ryan ULC, wants the freeze lifted. His best reason is quiet overpayment. Owners whose property rose less than the local average, or fell, have paid more than they otherwise would, sometimes thousands of dollars a year, because the base never moved. He told The Globe and Mail the biggest problem is education and transparency: people do not know, and if they did there would be outrage. He has launched a campaign to end the pause.

Critics of lifting it warn, as The Globe and Mail reports, of explosive political cost. Owners whose property rose faster than their community’s average could face higher bills. The freeze did not stop municipalities from raising rates; it froze the values those rates use, normally reset every four years and phased in over four. MPAC was about to issue a 2020 reassessment when the pandemic hit.

Both sides share one roll: six years of bills on the fully phased-in 2016 value, now a decade old, after other pandemic rules ended. Sullivan’s campaign is the live push, and Ford’s government has left the 2020 order in place. MPAC, in that same account, says almost half of Ontario condo units are worth less than $500,000 as prices plunge, a change the frozen roll does not capture. Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-ontarios-taxing-problem-with-property-owners/)

> **Seven in ten Albertans plan to vote to keep the province in Canada.**

**What You Need to Know:** Seven in ten Albertans plan to vote to keep the province in Canada. An Ipsos poll for Global News, taken online from September 18 to 22, puts that share against 20 percent who would start a binding independence referendum on October 19. Ipsos calls a two-point drop from its late-spring poll statistically insignificant.

### Lead
**As referendum looms, 70% of Albertans want province to remain in Canada: Global News**
An Ipsos poll conducted online for Global News from September 18 to 22 interviewed 1,500 Canadian adults, including 600 Alberta residents, ahead of the October 19 referendum. Seven in ten Albertans said they plan to vote for Alberta to remain a province of Canada, down two points from Ipsos polling between May 28 and June 1, a change Ipsos calls statistically insignificant. Twenty percent said they would vote for Alberta to commence a binding independence referendum, with support highest among men at 25 percent, Gen Z respondents born from 1997 to 2012 at 28 percent, and Albertans outside Calgary and Edmonton at 28 percent. Ipsos Public Affairs senior vice-president Gregory Jack said the stay-or-go numbers have not really changed through the campaign, and that turnout matters because the side that wants to leave is more motivated than the side that wants to stay. Ipsos found 76 percent of Albertans know the ballot has several questions, and 62 percent plan to vote on all 10. Premier Danielle Smith added the separatism question on May 21 to a referendum announced February 19 that began with nine questions on immigration and the Constitution. Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12072083/alberta-referendum-ipsos-september-2026/)

**Senate plots its final week before elections with potential data center electricity vote: Roll Call**
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, Republican of South Dakota, told reporters Thursday that the Senate returns next week to finish business before the November midterms, with a test vote on the Ratepayer Protection Act front and center. The bill would require state regulators to consider standards so large data centers pay for electric-grid upgrades tied to rising electricity prices. The House passed it last week, 417 to 3, and Democrats blocked Senator Jon Husted, Republican of Ohio, from clearing it for President Donald Trump’s signature. Husted, whom Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales rates in a toss-up against Democratic former senator Sherrod Brown, said the president, House Democrats and Republicans, consumers, and the business community want the bill. Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, Democrat of New York, said Wednesday that Husted’s bill is voluntary and “a fraud,” and that the Democratic bill is mandatory and stronger. Source: [rollcall.com](https://rollcall.com/2026/09/25/senate-plots-its-final-week-before-elections-with-potential-data-center-electricity-vote/)

**Why so many Republicans are rejecting Trump’s AI vision for education: Vox**
Six months ago, first lady Melania Trump told a White House education summit to imagine an AI humanoid educator named Plato giving children classical studies at home. The administration’s showcase is Alpha School, whose student was a State of the Union guest: children there do reading and math on AI software for two hours a day, then workshops with adults the school calls guides rather than teachers. Alpha says students learn 2.6 times faster; Vox reports no outside researcher has verified that. After leaders at Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google DeepMind urged a slowdown, President Donald Trump called the panic a hoax and said whoever wins AI wins. Republican-led Florida, Iowa, and Utah have passed limits on AI and screens in schools, and Vox describes a fight inside the GOP over parental choice, innovation, and whether publicly funded schools must prove they work. Source: [vox.com](https://www.vox.com/technology/504061/ai-education-schools-trump-texas-alpha-screentime-vouchers-charters)

**GOP senators dismayed by Trump embrace of Xi after China helped Iran target US troops: The Hill**
Republican senators are expressing concern and dismay, The Hill reports, over President Trump’s welcome of Chinese President Xi Jinping to a two-day summit in Washington. The dismay follows word earlier this month that Iran used Chinese satellite imagery to target US troops in Jordan. Republican senators were told of deepening military cooperation between Iran and China. The Hill describes the Washington welcome as lavish. ### Both Sides: Sending the narrowed Strong Borders Act to committee
The House of Commons is resuming second reading of Bill C-2, the Strong Borders Act, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree’s package on the Canada–US border and related security measures. The motion would send the bill to the Standing Committee on Public Safety and National Security. The government has removed provisions that would have allowed law enforcement warrantless access, narrowing the text from the version first called for second reading on September 17, 2025.

Anandasangaree told the House in Thursday’s Question Period that since taking office last year the government has made “an unprecedented amount of legislative changes” for Canadians’ safety, citing Bill C-14 on bail and sentencing, Bill C-16 on victims’ rights, and Bill C-9 on community safety. Justice Minister Sean Fraser said the government is advancing legislation to fight serious crime and toughen the penal system, and would act on the advice of experts and police. The Hub reports that, with a majority government, the second-reading vote is not in doubt, and that the live questions are the shape of the bill that reaches committee and how long debate runs before the government moves it along.

Conservatives, as The Hub describes the fight, are pressing ministers on violent offences and sentencing, treating the border bill as part of an unfinished argument over crime rather than a file closed by bills already passed or in progress. That is the case the opposition is putting against letting the package move on the government’s timetable.

Both sides are working from the same order paper: C-2 leads Friday’s government business, ahead of Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne’s four tax motions, Bill C-28, the Canadian Space Launch Act, and Bill C-34, the Safe Social Media Act, with eight private members’ bills also on the order of precedence. The next step named in the debate is the motion to send the narrowed bill to the public safety committee. Source: [thehub.ca](https://thehub.ca/2026/09/25/parliament-today-strong-borders-act-returns-to-second-reading/?hubcta)

# Omni View North America
> **More than twenty-five thousand deportations to third countries are now blocked, changing where people can be sent.**

**What You Need to Know:** More than twenty-five thousand deportations to third countries are now blocked, changing where people can be sent. Attorney General Todd Blanche said the Justice Department will ask the Supreme Court to restore the policy after a Boston appeals court let its block take effect. The same morning, Xi Jinping was at the White House, where President Trump called this Xi’s second formal visit.

### Lead
**Blanche Vows Supreme Court Review in Third-Country Removal Case: Bloomberg Law News**
Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday that the Department of Justice will immediately ask the Supreme Court for relief, after the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit on third-country removals take effect. That ruling requires meaningful notice that a person will be sent to a country they are not connected to, and a chance to claim they would be persecuted there. Blanche wrote on X that the court acted without giving the government a chance to respond, “in the dark of night,” and blocked all third-country removals, which he called an entirely legal and invaluable tool to stem illegal immigration. A tracker from Refugees International and Human Rights First counts more than 25,000 people sent to 29 third countries; The Guardian, citing Third Country Deportation Watch, says that in many cases the country is Mexico, and that some people have been sent to the Central African Republic and South Sudan. Lawyers for the class said they had learned officials were preparing a Thursday flight from Louisiana toward African countries, and that officials had argued removals could continue because the September 18 opinion had no mandate yet. Federal immigration law allows removal to a country other than the country of origin when removal to the designated country is impractical, inadvisable, or impossible. Source: [news.bloomberglaw.com](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/blanche-vows-supreme-court-review-in-third-country-removal-case)

### Across the Region
**Institutional failures, dismissed warning signs factors in deaths of eight children, report says: The Globe and Mail**
A report published Thursday by the National Association of Women and the Law and law professors at the University of Sherbrooke says institutional failures, and warnings from mothers that officials dismissed, played a role in the deaths of eight children in five cases in Canada. The authors write that significant warning signs were present before each death but did not bring adequate protective action, and that mothers — and in one case a grandmother — who identified safety risks were disbelieved or penalized while the children stayed in contact with fathers whose abusive conduct institutions already knew. In a 2019 case in Granby, Quebec, a seven-year-old girl was found unconscious in her room and later died in hospital after placement in her father’s custody; her grandmother had warned of a serious risk of sexual abuse and then lost custody after being seen as hostile for reporting those dangers. The report says the director of youth protection did not push for home visits and that nothing followed a month out of school; it says the stepmother was found guilty of manslaughter and false imprisonment and the father pleaded guilty to false imprisonment. The authors are scheduled to present the report on Parliament Hill Thursday morning with Liberal MP Lisa Hepfner, whose private member’s bill would, with some exceptions, bar a court from considering an allegation that a spouse deliberately manipulated a child into resisting the other spouse. Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-institutional-failures-warning-signs-deaths-of-eight-children-report/)

**Kentucky Supreme Court upholds opinion on Fayette Co. judge’s impeachment: WKYT**
The Kentucky Supreme Court said Thursday it will not change its April 6 opinion voiding the impeachment of Fayette County Circuit Judge Julie Muth Goodman, after the justices taking part split evenly and court rules left that order standing. In April the court had ruled 5-1 to halt the proceedings. The Kentucky House passed an impeachment resolution on March 20, claiming Goodman abused judicial discretion and authority. Thursday’s order keeps the General Assembly from any further impeachment proceedings in this matter, while a separate judicial conduct investigation can still go forward. One case in the petition is the 2020 hit-and-run death of Tammy Botkin: Goodman dismissed a murder indictment against Cornell Thomas II, and in December the Kentucky Court of Appeals unanimously ruled to re-indict him. Source: [wkyt.com](https://www.wkyt.com/2026/09/24/kentucky-supreme-court-upholds-opinion-fayette-co-judges-impeachment/)

### Also Today
**Canada’s Carney considered chance Trump might use military force to make it join US: NYT: The Straits Times**
Prime Minister Mark Carney told the New York Times, in an interview published late September 23, that a U.S. military effort to make Canada part of the United States is a “tail risk” Canada must prepare for, not the base case, after trade talks broke down on August 21. Source: [straitstimes.com](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/canadas-carney-considered-chance-trump-might-use-military-force-to-make-it-join-us-nyt)

**Canada’s Capital Bids Good Riddance to Trump Avenue as Tensions With U.S. Rise: The New York Times**
Ottawa’s City Council decided a street should no longer be named for President Trump, the New York Times reports, after he signed an executive order changing Lake Ontario to Lake America. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/23/us/ottawa-canada-renaming-trump-avenue.html)

**Mexico Calls to Reduce Automotive Tariffs to USA: MEXICONOW**
Mexico called for lower automotive tariffs on shipments to the United States. Source: [mexico-now.com](https://mexico-now.com/mexico-calls-to-reduce-automotive-tariffs-to-usa/)

**Healey rolls out $2.24B spending plan as federal cuts loom over Massachusetts: masslive.com**
Healey pitched a $2.24 billion spending package in Massachusetts to shore up health care, SNAP, and affordability as federal cuts loom. Source: [masslive.com](https://www.masslive.com/politics/2026/09/healey-pitches-224b-spending-package-to-shore-up-healthcare-snap-and-affordability.html)

### The Region and the World
**Xi says China and US must ensure AI ‘is always under human control’ as Trump touts ‘great friendship’ before White House talks: The Guardian**
President Xi Jinping arrived at the White House on Thursday morning for talks expected to cover trade, AI, Taiwan, and more, The Guardian reports. Donald Trump said Xi is the first Chinese leader to make a second formal visit to the White House, and that the two have “forged a truly great friendship” since Trump was first elected in 2016. Trump said this is the first time he and Xi are meeting at the White House, and that a lot has changed since Xi was last here. The New York Times describes the trip as Xi’s first visit to the White House in a decade, during what the Times calls Trump’s unexpected turn from a hard line on China. In the front row sat Vice President JD Vance and Usha Vance, Ivanka Trump and her daughter Arabella, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live/2026/sep/24/trump-xi-jinping-china-ai-trade-summit-latest-news-updates)

### Both Sides: Impeaching a judge over her rulings
Kentucky’s Supreme Court has left in place an order that stops lawmakers from continuing the impeachment of Fayette Circuit Judge Julie Muth Goodman. The fight is whether the General Assembly may remove a judge for her rulings, or whether those disputes belong in appeals and judicial discipline.

The House says Goodman abused judicial discretion and authority, and it passed an impeachment resolution on March 20. After Franklin Circuit Judge Phillip J. Shepherd ruled on March 31 that the proceedings were null and void, lawmakers told the Lexington Herald-Leader he has no constitutional authority to void an impeachment and that a Senate trial should still happen. Their best reason is institutional: impeachment, they argue, is a legislative power a trial court cannot cancel.

The Supreme Court says this petition was not a lawful impeachment because it was never sworn or verified by affidavit, as state law requires. The justices said the allegations were disagreements over rulings in six cases, not impeachable offenses, and that such complaints must go through appeals and the judicial conduct commission. They warned that impeaching judges over controversial decisions would violate the separation of powers, threaten judicial independence, and could lead to what the court called tyrannical control of the courts. They also said the process denied Goodman due process, because five of the six cases were still pending and ethics rules barred her from publicly defending her decisions.

Both sides are contesting the same March 20 resolution, and neither disputes that a separate judicial conduct investigation into Goodman can still move forward. Thursday’s order records an even split among the justices taking part, so the April 6 opinion stands and the injunction against further impeachment proceedings remains.

### Progress Watch
The day had none.

# Omni View North America
> **Trump signed a Greenland security deal that expands the U.S. military presence, not U.S. control.**

**What You Need to Know:** President Donald Trump signed a security agreement on Greenland that widens the U.S. military presence without taking control of the territory. In Washington, Missouri’s congressional map is back at the Supreme Court, the White House is defending a ban on several news outlets, and Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Greg Casar are introducing a bill to ban artificial superintelligence. In Canada, Squamish rejected a $142 million LNG agreement, and Prime Minister Mark Carney announced C$100 million in aid for Palestine.

### What This Show Covers
If you want one region, every day, told straight, this is that brief: what was decided, what happened, what it changes and for whom. Each edition also sets out one contested question, with the strongest case on each side, and one measurable sign of progress when the day’s reporting contains one.

This desk covers the United States and Canada, and United States–Mexico affairs: the border, tariffs, and the trade pact the countries share. Mexico’s domestic politics are not this desk’s. A story from anywhere else is here only for a consequence inside the United States or Canada, and that consequence is stated first.

The brief is read by Mira, the network’s AI host. Stories are chosen and written by software from named newsrooms, and every item names its source. It will not take a side: every claim is attributed, and no party, government, or people is praised or mocked.

Other Omni View desks, and Omni View Top World News, cover the world beyond this region.

Omni View North America is part of the Nerra Network, an independent, ad-free network of shows at nerranetwork.com. You can find it there — an invitation to listen, not a sales pitch.

### Lead
**Trump Once Vowed to ‘Own’ Greenland. He Settled for Something Much Less.: The New York Times**
President Donald Trump signed a security agreement with Denmark and Greenland that expands the U.S. military presence but stops short of taking control of the territory, The New York Times reports. The Times says the agreement was reached on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly amid prolonged tensions, and that it falls short of earlier demands by Trump to own Greenland. The Associated Press also reported the signing of the U.S.-Denmark-Greenland security deal at the United Nations. For Denmark and Greenland, the territory is not transferred; for the United States, the change is a larger military footprint, not ownership. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/topic/subject/united-states-politics-and-government)

### Across the Region
**Battle over Missouri's congressional map reaches US Supreme Court for third time: Reuters**
Challengers to a redrawn congressional map in Missouri, which Reuters describes as aimed at favoring Republicans, returned to the U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday and urged the court to halt the map’s use in November’s midterm elections. Reuters reports that a St. Louis-based federal court again ordered the map reinstated, despite two previous Supreme Court orders to the contrary. Reuters headlines the filing as the third time the battle has reached the Supreme Court. Source: [reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/battle-over-missouris-congressional-map-reaches-us-supreme-court-third-time-2026-09-23/)

**B.C.'s District of Squamish rejects $142M Woodfibre LNG deal: CBC News**
The District of Squamish in British Columbia has, CBC News reports. CBC says local leaders cited concerns over community benefits and environmental impacts, and that the decision affects the project’s development timeline. Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/lite/news/canada)

**Labour law changes would bring 'sunlight' to collective bargaining: jobs minister: BNN Bloomberg**
Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu says proposed changes to the Canada Labour Code will increase transparency in collective bargaining, BNN Bloomberg reports. BNN says the bill includes measures to address work stoppages and project approvals. Unions have raised concerns about potential impacts on strike rights, BNN reports. The changes are a proposal, not law. Source: [bnnbloomberg.ca](https://www.bnnbloomberg.ca/business/politics/)

### The Region and the World
**Canada is giving C$100 million in international aid for Palestine, says Carney: Reuters**
Prime Minister Mark Carney announced C$100 million in Canadian assistance for Palestine during U.N. General Assembly events, Reuters reports. Reuters says the aid focuses on humanitarian support. The sum is a Canadian spending decision, made in New York, directed outside the country. Source: [reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/canada/)

### Both Sides: A ban on artificial superintelligence
The decision before Congress is whether the United States should ban artificial superintelligence, pause development of advanced artificial-intelligence systems, and create a Department of Artificial Intelligence. Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Greg Casar are introducing legislation that would do all three, the Associated Press reports. It is a proposal being introduced, not a law that has been passed.

Sanders’s case, as the AP reports it, starts with risk. He argues that the potential dangers demand immediate action and international cooperation. The AP says the proposal comes as prominent artificial-intelligence executives and researchers increasingly warn about potentially catastrophic risks from rapidly advancing systems, and that Congress has struggled to agree on safeguards. The reason he puts first is that those dangers justify a ban, a pause, a new department, and cooperation beyond one country.

The case against that approach, as the AP attributes it to President Donald Trump, is competitive position. He has pushed back on new regulations and emphasized maintaining an advantage over China. The reason in that reported position is the edge over China, and resistance to new rules, rather than a pause on advanced systems or a ban on superintelligence.

The fact neither account disputes is that Sanders and Casar are introducing a bill, and that it is not yet law. What happens next is that introduction. The AP frames the open choice as Sanders’s call for a ban and international cooperation against Trump’s reported resistance to new regulation in the name of an advantage over China.

### Progress Watch
The day had none.
